findings.title: Truth-framed transmission
findings.claim: The repeated bi-l-haqq can be heard as holding the sending and the arrival of the message within one truth frame; the paired glad-tidings and warning offices inform their audience while leaving its response open. Transmission integrity is a bounded inference from this framing, not an explicit technical claim of textual non-distortion.
findings.mechanism: The focus repeats haqq across a causative sending and an intransitive arrival. Supplied wider connections echo truth descending and falsehood departing, identify the public reach and warning function of the message, and show that hearers may still refuse it; these contacts return through the focus's truth nouns, descent forms, and paired messenger roles.
findings.reader_payoff: The repeated truth phrase reads as a relation between source and arrival, while glad tidings and warning describe communicative work rather than control over what hearers do with it.
findings.containment: This reading keeps the ordinary truth, descent, sending, glad-tidings, and warning senses intact. It does not prove perfect textual preservation, erase rejection, or claim that the messenger controls assent; 67:9 preserves refusal as a live response.

epistemic.reason: The focus wording and trusted support ground the source/arrival relation. Legacy duplicate supports and external connections without target morphology qualify the wider synthesis; the non-distortion implication remains abductive rather than demonstrated.

branch_activations.resulting_reading: The source-side sending and arrival-side descent can be heard together under one truth relation.
branch_activations.boundary: This does not convert haqq into the excluded fabric or speech collocation, nor prove a technical theory of textual preservation.

epistemic.reason: The originating retrospective support is legacy-unbound. The supplied 25:32 Arabic gives a concrete independent trigger, but its morphology is not supplied, so pacing remains a qualified wider resonance.

findings.claim: The wider challenge-and-answer context lets the focus's sent addressee be heard as a human messenger while the message itself descends; 17:95's angelic envoy remains explicitly counterfactual.
findings.mechanism: Connections at 17:93 and 17:95 return through the focus addressee, sending verb, and Form I descent. The first states the human-messenger demand, while the second contrasts earthly angels with an angel sent down from heaven only under that condition.
findings.reader_payoff: The focus can hold two coordinated acts in view: a human messenger is sent to people, and the message descends. The angel contrast sharpens the distinction without adding an actual angelic envoy.
findings.containment: The human reading belongs to the referent of the sent addressee, not to the lexical meaning of mubashshiran; that participle retains its good-tidings sense. No actual angel descent is claimed.

epistemic.reason: Both connections supply exact target Arabic but no target morphology; the human-referent and conditional contrast are clear contextual contacts, not a lexical replacement of the focus wording.
